rules.message: `any` type used — defeats TypeScript's type checking for this value. Replace with a concrete type, a generic parameter, or `unknown` plus a type guard if the shape is genuinely dynamic. Two cases where `any` is the RIGHT call rather than a violation: an in-progress JS-to-TypeScript migration, where each `any` marks a boundary still to be typed and deleting them is the plan; and a generic constraint position `unknown` cannot satisfy (`<T extends any[]>`). A project that ships those deliberately is disagreeing with this rule, not breaking it. A file whose first 8 lines carry a machine-generated banner comment (`@generated`, `auto-generated`/`autogenerated`, `automatically generated`, `code generated by`, `this file is generated`, `this file was generated`, `openapi-generator`) is skipped WHOLE: an `any` there is the generator's output, so advice to fix the line is undone by the next regeneration. That banner list is COMPILED INTO this rule and does NOT read `vocabulary.generatedFileMarkers` — that config key reaches only the dead-code analyses (`unimported-export`, `dead-candidates`), so a house generator whose output carries a different banner — or no banner at all — is still flagged here, and the answer in either case is an `exclude` entry for its path.

`as any` / `as unknown as` cast — a hard escape from type checking (`as any` disables it, `as unknown as X` force-casts through an incompatible type). Prefer a type guard, a properly-typed API, or `unknown` plus a narrowing check. Plain `as X` to a compatible type is not flagged. The cast is the RIGHT call in two cases: a third-party package whose own type declarations are wrong or incomplete, where an audited one-line cast at the call site beats shipping a patched copy of them; and a force-cast into a branded/nominal type the checker has no constructor for. A project that permits those deliberately disagrees with this rule rather than violating it. A file whose first 8 lines carry a machine-generated banner comment (`@generated`, `auto-generated`/`autogenerated`, `automatically generated`, `code generated by`, `this file is generated`, `this file was generated`, `openapi-generator`) is skipped WHOLE: a cast there is the generator's output, so rewriting it is undone by the next regeneration. That banner list is COMPILED INTO this rule and does NOT read `vocabulary.generatedFileMarkers` — that config key reaches only the dead-code analyses (`unimported-export`, `dead-candidates`), so a house generator whose output carries a different banner — or no banner at all — is still flagged here, and the answer in either case is an `exclude` entry for its path.

useEffect callback declared async — React ignores the returned Promise and no cleanup function can be returned; a rejection becomes unhandled. Move the async work into an inner async function or IIFE: `useEffect(() => { void doAsync(); }, deps)`.

An `on<Event>={async ...}` JSX handler (or `on<Event>: async ...` handler-map property) has an `await` but no try/catch — a rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection. Add try/catch (or `.catch()`) inside the handler.

A decimal-fraction or negative-exponent numeric literal compared with `==`/`===`/`!=`/`!==` — IEEE754 floats don't represent most decimal fractions exactly, so equality on a computed value is unreliable even against an exactly-written literal (`0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3`; SonarQube's S1244 flags all float equality for the same reason). Use an epsilon comparison (`Math.abs(a - b) < eps`), integer minor units, or a decimal library instead. Money-named comparisons (`price`/`amount`/`balance`/`fee`/`cost`) are covered separately by `db/float-money-compare` and are not double-flagged here.

A constant-result comparison: `x === NaN`/`x == NaN` is always false and `x !== NaN`/`x != NaN` is always true (NaN never equals anything, including itself — use `Number.isNaN(x)`), and strict `x === []`/`x === {}` compares object identity against a freshly-allocated literal, so it is always false (`!==` always true — use `.length === 0` / `Object.keys(x).length === 0`). Loose `x == []` is deliberately NOT matched (coercion can make it true — `0 == []` is true). Core ESLint's `use-isnan` covers the NaN half when ESLint is configured — zzop's value here is catching it with zero lint config.

A numeric-looking string literal compared with `<`/`>`/`<=`/`>=` — string comparison is lexicographic, not numeric (`'10' < '9'` is `true`; `'10.0.0' < '9.0.0'` is `true`). Convert both sides with `Number(...)` first, or use a semver library for version strings.

.toFixed() returns a STRING — using its result in `-`/`*`/`/`/`%` arithmetic silently coerces back to a number and loses the rounding/formatting intent (string concatenation via `+` is a separate, usually-intentional display case and is NOT flagged here). Do the arithmetic first and call `.toFixed()` last, for display only, or wrap in `Number(x.toFixed(2))` if re-quantizing is genuinely intended.

A timezone/epoch pitfall in `Date` handling: a date-only ISO string (`new Date('2024-01-15')`) parses as UTC midnight while the slash form (`new Date('2024/01/15')`) parses in local time — the two disagree by a day near timezone boundaries; a 10-digit literal passed to `new Date(...)` is a UNIX-SECONDS timestamp, but `Date` expects milliseconds and silently yields a 1970 date; and a day-length constant (`86400000`, `24*60*60*1000`) appearing as the RIGHT-hand operand of a `+`/`-` inside `new Date(...)` — the shape `new Date(<expr> + 86400000)` — shifts that value by exactly 24 hours, which is not a calendar day across DST transitions (23/25-hour days), and is an outright `Date`-to-string coercion bug when `<expr>` is itself a `Date`. The epoch veto is STRUCTURAL, not a token blocklist: no closing paren may appear between `new Date(` and the operator, so an operand that is a call result (`Date.now()`, `.getTime()`, `Date.parse(...)`, `Date.UTC(...)`, `.valueOf()`, `Number(...)`) or a parenthesized subexpression (`new Date((a + b) + 86400000)`) cannot match at all. Also out of scope: the mirrored operand order (`86400000 + d`), a multiplicative days-to-ms conversion (`* 86400000`), and any day arithmetic with no `new Date(` head (`Date.now() - 7 * 86400000`) — epoch/UTC milliseconds are DST-safe by construction, and all six measured findings of the earlier, wider form were exactly those shapes. Two residuals, stated honestly: a bare identifier that happens to hold epoch ms (`new Date(startMs + 86400000)`) is file-locally indistinguishable from a `Date`-valued one; and the unary-coercion form `new Date(+d + 86400000)` carries no closing paren, so it still fires even though `+d` is epoch ms exactly as `.getTime()` is. Use a date library's `addDays`, or keep the whole computation in epoch/UTC space.

`.forEach(async ...)` — `forEach` ignores the promises its callback returns: the loop call itself resolves before any callback body finishes, callback errors become unhandled promise rejections, and there is no way to await completion. Use a `for...of` loop with `await`, or `Promise.all(items.map(async ...))` if the iterations are independent. `.map(async ...)` is a related but different defect (an unawaited array of promises) covered separately by `reliability/map-async-no-promise-all`.

`new Promise(async (resolve, reject) => ...)` — an async executor function's own thrown errors/rejections are swallowed, because the `Promise` constructor never observes the promise the async executor itself returns; it also usually signals a redundant wrapper, since the async function already returns a promise. Core ESLint's `no-async-promise-executor` already covers this when configured — zzop's value here is catching it with zero lint config.

`parseInt(...)` called with a single argument — the radix parameter documents intent and guards against legacy surprises (`'0x10'` auto-parses as hex; old engines treated a leading-zero string as octal). Pass an explicit radix, e.g. `parseInt(x, 10)`. Omitting it is the RIGHT call when the argument is a string this code produced or already validated as decimal digits: no `0x` prefix can reach it, and the leading-zero octal reading was dropped from the language in ES5, so the radix is ceremony rather than a guard there. This scan only looks at the literal argument span up to the closing `)`; a nested call (`parseInt(getVal())`) is not flagged — a documented miss rather than a guess. Core ESLint's `radix` rule covers this too but is not in its `recommended` config.
